latin.65:
CAPUT VIII.
Argumenta D. Gar. ex Rom. V. versibus 14. 15. 16. 17. 18. 19. expenduntur.

Ex versu 14. hunc nectit Syllogismum. Ea est inter typum & τὸ ἀντίτυπον convenientia, ut quod in re per typum representata exhibetur, illud in typo praecessisse oportuerit. Atqui Adamus proponitur ut typus Christi in iis quae ad rationem iustificationis pertinent; ut nempe simili modo condemnationem habeamus in Adamo, quo iustificationem habemus in Christo. Itaque cum ea sit ratio iustificationis nostrae per Christum, ut eius iustitia nobis per imputationem communicata iustificemur, sive pro iustis habeamur apud Deum; Eam etiam oportet esse condemnationis per Adamum nostrae rationem, ut illius peccato nobis per imputationem communicato condemnemur, & pro peccatoribus ac reis habeamur apud Deum. Principio quacunque sit hujus argumenti vis, eo nonnisi consequens seu mediata imputatio concludi potest. Nam ut imputatio iustitiae sequitur fidem nostram, sic imputatio peccati sequitur corruptionem nostram. Hoc si sufficit, pax esto.
latin.66: Deinde nullo negotio dissolvi potest hoc argumentum. Ad majorem enim quod attinet, propositio, Quod in re per typum representata exhibetur, illud in typo praecessisse oportuit. Eget hac limitatione, si nempe ad id representandum typus fuit comparatus. Nam alioqui saepenumero multa in re representata exhibita fuerunt, quae non potuerunt uno typo representari; quapropter multi ad eandem rem adumbrandam adhibiti sunt. Deinde etiam adhibita illa limitatione propositio vera non est, nisi quantum pati potest ejus rei, quae typus est, natura, servata inter Typum & τὸ ἀντίτυπον, umbram & corpus differentia. Itaque melior est a typo ad rem adumbratam, quam ab hac ad illam argumentatio.
latin.67: Ad minorem autem quod spectat, jam aliquoties negavimus urgeri debere similitudinem in modo, quo ab Adamo condemnationem, & a Christo iustificationem habemus. Idque cum autoritate magnorum virorum, tum aliquot exemplis comprobavimus. Audi, si placet, Calvinum, Porro duas hic differentias inter Christum & Adamum notare operae pretium est: quas non ideo praeteriit Apostolus, quia negligendas censeret, sed quia praesentis argumenti nihil referebat eas enumerare. Prior est quod peccato Adae non per solam imputationem damnamur, ac si alieni peccati exigeretur a nobis poena: sed ideo poenam eius sustinemus, quia & culpae sumus rei, quatenus scilicet natura nostra in ipso vitiata, iniquitatis reatu astringitur apud Deum. At per Christi iustitiam alio modo in salutem restituimur: neque enim ideo nobis accepta fertur, quia intra nos sit: sed quod Christum ipsum cum bonis suis omnibus, Patris largitate nobis donatum possidemus. Itaque donum iustitiae, non qualitatem qua nos Deus imbuat, ut perperam quidam interpretantur, sed gratuitam iustitiae imputationem significat.
latin.68: Placet-ne etiam audire Rodolphum Gualterum? Sensus ergo est, in hoc quidem comparari inter se posse Adamum & Christum, quod uterque quod suum erat in suos propagarit. In caeteris vero Multiplex esse discrimen, neque eandem esse rationem offensae aut peccati per Adamum invecti, & beneficii nobis in Christo exhibiti &c. & paulo post. Videtur autem duplex discrimen his verbis annotari, ut primo quidem Natura corrupta & gratia Dei opponantur, eo quod Adam quidem propter naturae corruptionem, quam ex suo lapsu contraxit, peccatum in omnes posteros propagarit, adeo ut peccatores ex ipso matris utero nascamur: Christus vero nobis ex gratia datus sit, ut eius iustitia sive obedientia in multos, id est, in omnes redundaret. Quod ergo peccatores & propter peccatum morti obnoxii sumus, hoc ex natura ceu proprium habemus: quod vero iusti & vitae consortes facti sumus, id gratuitum Dei beneficium est, qui Filii sui iustitiam nobis imputat propter fidem, qua hunc apprehendimus. His duobus tertium adiungam Petrum Martyrem Com. in Rom. 5. Vs. 14. ad verba qui est typus futuri. Similitudo haec accipienda est in genere quod sicut omnes ab Adamo, ita omnes a Christo iuxta ordinem suum pendeant: quodque quemadmodum alter meritus est suis omnibus, ita etiam alter. Sed particulariter & quoad species magnum est discrimen. Nam Adamus peccatum, mortem, & damnationem invexit: Christus vero iustitiam, vitam & gratiam. Est etiam discrimen in propagatione. Adamus enim mala sua per carnis generationem in homines transfudit. Christus autem per fidem. Ideo Paulus cum dixisset, Adamum typum fuisse futuri, quasi per correctionem subiicit. At non ut peccatum, ita & donum. Quamobrem inter Adamum & Christum potius analogia quaedam & proportio, quam vera similitudo constituenda est. Vides nos Magnorum virorum doctrinam adversus D. Garissolii impetum defendere. Noli nos igitur quaeso, candide lector, novitatis damnare.
latin.69: II. Ex Vs. 15. At non ut lapsus, ita etiam donum &c. sic colligit; Qui Adami actuali peccato morti facti sunt obnoxii, illi poenam ferunt illius peccati, adeoque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur. Atqui omnes homines actuali Adami peccato facti sunt morti obnoxii. Ergo omnes homines ferunt poenam illius peccati, adeoque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur. Facilis est responsio. Qui Adami actuali peccato morti facti sunt obnoxii proxime seu immediate, illi poenam ferunt illius peccati proxime seu immediate. Qui eo peccato facti sunt morti obnoxii tantum remote seu mediate, hoc est, mediante corruptione, illi ferunt poenas illius peccati tantum remote seu mediate, hoc est, mediante corruptione. Atqui omnes homines actuali Adami peccato facti sunt morti obnoxii proxime seu immediate, Nego: mediante corruptione, Concedo. Ergo omnes homines ferunt poenam illius peccati, adeoque peccatum illud ipsis imputatur, immediate, nego: mediante corruptione nobis inhaerente, Concedo. Nonne omnia D. Gar. argumenta hac una fidelia dealbari possunt?
latin.70: Deinde, inquit, opponuntur ab Apostolo τὸ παράπτωμα Adami & τὸ χάρισμα Christi. At per χάρισμα intelligitur iustitia illa Christi, quae gratiosa imputatione fit nostra, & quae sanctificationem, sive iustitiam inhaerentem ex se necessario fundit. Ergo & παράπτωμα intelligitur peccatum illud Adami, quod imputatione nostrum fit, & quod corruptio nostra naturalis necessario & infallibiliter sequitur. Omnino opponuntur ab Apostolo τὸ παράπτωμα Adami & τὸ χάρισμα Christi. Quid inde sequitur? Nonne jam aliquoties argumento ducto ab hac oppositione occurrimus? Caeterum aut anomalus est hic syllogismus, nec vim ullam concludendi habet, aut omissa est propositio, quae si universaliter, ut debet, concipiatur, erit falsa procul dubio. Admonet autem nos oppositio inter παράπτωμα Adami & χάρισμα Christi, longe aliter hoc nostrum esse quam illud. Non enim, ut hoc nostrum est dono Christi, sic illud est nostrum dono Adami. Alterum ergo alteri opponit Apostolus in modo quo fit nostrum. Quomodo igitur ex hac oppositione concludere potest D. G. utrumque eodem modo nostrum fieri? Dicet-ne imputationem, qua aliquid nostrum fit, alioqui non nostrum, esse donationem quandam. Est igitur Adami peccatum donum quoddam, non Adami, hic enim non imputat; sed, horresco pronuncians, ipsius Dei.

pass_a.65: Chapter eight opens: Garissoles's arguments from Romans 5:14–19 will be weighed. From verse 14 he joins this syllogism. There is a fit between type and antitype (τὸ ἀντίτυπον): what is shown in the thing the type represents must have come first in the type. But Adam is set as Christ's type in what belongs to the account of justification — namely that we have condemnation in Adam in a like way to justification in Christ. Therefore, since our justification through Christ means his righteousness is communicated to us by imputation so we are justified or counted just before God, our condemnation through Adam must mean his sin is communicated to us by imputation so we are condemned and counted sinners and guilt-bound before God. Placeus's first move: whatever force this argument has, it can conclude only consequent or mediate imputation. For as imputation of righteousness follows our faith, so imputation of sin follows our corruption. If that is enough, let there be peace.
pass_a.66: Next the argument can be dissolved without trouble. As to the major: the proposition 'What is shown in the thing represented by a type must have preceded in the type' needs this limit — if the type was in fact set up to represent that thing. Otherwise often many things appear in the represented matter that one type could not show, so several types are used to sketch the same thing. Even with that limit the proposition is true only as far as the nature of the type-thing can bear, keeping the difference between type and antitype, shadow and body. So arguing from type to the shadowed thing is better than from the thing back to the type.
pass_a.67: As to the minor: Placeus has already often denied that the likeness of mode must be pressed — the mode by which we have condemnation from Adam and justification from Christ. He has confirmed this by great men's authority and by examples. Hear Calvin if you will: it is worth marking two differences here between Christ and Adam; the Apostle did not skip them as negligible, but because listing them did not serve the present argument. First: we are not damned by Adam's sin through imputation alone, as if another's sin's penalty were exacted from us; we bear his penalty because we are also guilty of fault, inasmuch as our nature corrupted in him is bound before God under iniquity's guilt. But by Christ's righteousness we are restored to salvation another way: it is not credited to us because it is inside us, but because by the Father's bounty we possess Christ himself with all his goods. So the gift of righteousness does not mean a quality God pours into us (as some wrongly take it) but the free imputation of righteousness.
pass_a.68: Will you also hear Rudolph Gualther? The sense is that Adam and Christ can be compared in this — each propagated what was his into his own. In the rest the difference is manifold, and the account of the offense or sin brought in through Adam is not the same as the benefit shown us in Christ, and so on. And a little later: a double difference seems marked in these words, so that first corrupt nature and God's grace are opposed — because Adam, from the nature-corruption he contracted in his fall, propagated sin into all posterity so we are born sinners from the mother's womb; but Christ is given us by grace so his righteousness or obedience overflows into the many, that is into all. That we are sinners and death-liable for sin we have as our own from nature; that we are made just and life-partners is God's free benefit, who imputes his Son's righteousness to us for the faith by which we grasp him. To these two Placeus adds a third, Peter Martyr on Romans 5:14 at 'who is the type of the one to come': this likeness is to be taken in the genus — all hang from Adam, all from Christ, each in his order; and as the one merited for all his own, so also the other. But in particular and as to species the difference is great. Adam brought in sin, death, and damnation; Christ righteousness, life, and grace. There is also a difference in propagation: Adam poured his evils into humans by fleshly generation; Christ by faith. So when Paul had said Adam was type of the one to come, he almost corrects: but not as the sin, so also the gift. Therefore between Adam and Christ one should set an analogy and proportion rather than true likeness. You see Placeus defending the great men's teaching against Garissoles's assault. So do not, candid reader, damn us for novelty.
pass_a.69: Second, from verse 15, 'But not as the fall, so also the gift' and so on, Garissoles gathers: those made death-liable by Adam's actual sin bear that sin's penalty, and so that sin is imputed to them; but all humans were made death-liable by Adam's actual sin; therefore all bear that penalty and that sin is imputed to them. Easy reply. Those made death-liable by Adam's actual sin proximately or immediately bear that penalty proximately or immediately. Those made death-liable by that sin only remotely or mediately — that is, by intervening corruption — bear that penalty only remotely or mediately, by intervening corruption. But that all were made death-liable by Adam's actual sin proximately or immediately: I deny; by intervening corruption: I grant. Therefore that all bear that penalty and that sin is imputed to them immediately: I deny; by corruption inhering in us: I grant. Cannot all Garissoles's arguments be whitewashed with this one brush?
pass_a.70: Next, Garissoles says, the Apostle sets Adam's παράπτωμα over against Christ's χάρισμα. But by χάρισμα is meant that righteousness of Christ which becomes ours by gracious imputation and which necessarily pours out from itself sanctification or inhering righteousness. Therefore by παράπτωμα is meant that Adam-sin which becomes ours by imputation and which our natural corruption necessarily and infallibly follows. Yes, the Apostle does set Adam's παράπτωμα and Christ's χάρισμα opposite. What follows? Have we not already met this opposition-argument several times? Besides, either this syllogism is irregular and has no concluding force, or a premise is missing which, if framed universally as it should be, will doubtless be false. The opposition between Adam's παράπτωμα and Christ's χάρισμα warns us that this 'ours' is far otherwise than that. For it is not that as this is ours by Christ's gift, so that is ours by Adam's gift. So the Apostle opposes the one to the other in the mode by which it becomes ours. How then can Garissoles conclude from this opposition that both become ours the same way? Will he say that imputation, by which something otherwise not ours becomes ours, is a kind of donation? Then Adam's sin is a kind of gift — not Adam's, for he does not impute, but — I shudder to say it — God's own.

65: CAPUT VIII. The arguments of D. Garissoles from Romans 5, verses 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 19 are examined.

From verse 14 he joins this syllogism: There is this agreement between the type and the antitype (τὸ ἀντίτυπον), that what is exhibited in the thing represented by the type must have gone before in the type. But Adam is proposed as the type of Christ in those things that belong to the account of justification — namely that we should have condemnation in Adam in a like way to that in which we have justification in Christ (Romans 5:14). Therefore, since the account of our justification through Christ is that, his righteousness being communicated to us by imputation, we are justified, or are counted just before God, that must also be the account of our condemnation through Adam: that, his sin being communicated to us by imputation, we are condemned, and are counted sinners and guilty before God. First, whatever force this argument has, only consequent or mediate imputation can be concluded from it. For as the imputation of righteousness follows our faith, so the imputation of sin follows our corruption. If this is enough, let there be peace.
66: Next, this argument can be dissolved without any trouble. For as to the major: the proposition "What is exhibited in the thing represented by a type must have preceded in the type" needs this limitation — if, that is, the type was set up to represent that thing. For otherwise often many things have been exhibited in the represented matter which could not be represented by one type; and for that reason several have been employed to sketch the same thing. Then even when that limitation is applied, the proposition is not true except so far as the nature of the thing which is the type can bear, the difference between Type and antitype (τὸ ἀντίτυπον), shadow and body, being kept. Therefore argumentation from the type to the thing shadowed is better than from this latter back to the former.
67: But as to the minor: we have already denied several times that the likeness must be pressed in the mode by which we have condemnation from Adam and justification from Christ. And we have confirmed this both by the authority of great men and by several examples. Hear Calvin, if you please: "Further, it is worth noting here two differences between Christ and Adam: which the Apostle did not omit because he judged them negligible, but because it did not serve the present argument to enumerate them. The first is that we are not damned by Adam's sin through imputation alone, as if the penalty of another's sin were being exacted from us: but we therefore bear his penalty because we are also guilty of the fault, inasmuch as our nature, corrupted in him, is bound before God under the guilt of iniquity. But by Christ's righteousness we are restored to salvation in another way: for it is not therefore credited to us because it is within us, but because we possess Christ himself with all his goods, given to us by the Father's bounty. And so the gift of righteousness signifies not a quality with which God imbues us, as some wrongly interpret, but the free imputation of righteousness."
68: Does it please you also to hear Rudolph Gualther? "The sense, then, is that Adam and Christ can indeed be compared with each other in this, that each propagated into his own what was his. But in the rest there is a manifold difference, and the account of the offense or sin brought in through Adam is not the same as that of the benefit exhibited to us in Christ," and so on. And a little later: "But a double difference seems to be noted in these words, so that first corrupt Nature and the grace of God are opposed, because Adam indeed, on account of the corruption of nature which he contracted from his fall, propagated sin into all posterity, so that we are born sinners from the very womb of our mother: but Christ was given to us by grace, so that his righteousness or obedience should overflow into the many, that is, into all. Therefore that we are sinners and liable to death because of sin, we have from nature as our own: but that we have been made just and sharers of life is the free benefit of God, who imputes to us the righteousness of his Son because of the faith by which we apprehend him." To these two I will add a third, Peter Martyr, Commentary on Romans 5:14, at the words "who is the type of the one to come" (Romans 5:14): "This likeness is to be taken in the genus, that as all depend on Adam, so all depend on Christ according to their order: and that as the one has merited for all who are his, so also the other. But particularly and as to the species there is a great difference. For Adam brought in sin, death, and damnation: but Christ righteousness, life, and grace. There is also a difference in the propagation. For Adam poured his evils into men by the generation of the flesh. But Christ by faith. Therefore when Paul had said that Adam was the type of the one to come, he subjoins as if by correction: But not as the sin, so also the gift (Romans 5:15). Wherefore between Adam and Christ an analogy and proportion of a certain kind, rather than a true likeness, is to be established." You see us defending the teaching of great men against the assault of D. Garissoles. Do not therefore, I ask, candid reader, condemn us for novelty.
69: II. From verse 15, "But not as the fall, so also the gift," and so on (Romans 5:15), he gathers thus: Those who have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them. But all men have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin. Therefore all men bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them. The reply is easy. Those who have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin proximately or immediately bear the penalty of that sin proximately or immediately. Those who by that sin have been made liable to death only remotely or mediately — that is, by intervening corruption — bear the penalties of that sin only remotely or mediately, that is, by intervening corruption. But that all men have been made liable to death by Adam's actual sin proximately or immediately — I deny; by intervening corruption — I grant. Therefore that all men bear the penalty of that sin, and therefore that sin is imputed to them, immediately — I deny; by the corruption inhering in us — I grant. Cannot all the arguments of D. Garissoles be whitewashed with this one brush?
70: Next, he says, the Apostle sets opposite Adam's παράπτωμα and Christ's χάρισμα (Romans 5:15). But by χάρισμα is understood that righteousness of Christ which becomes ours by gracious imputation, and which necessarily pours forth from itself sanctification, or inhering righteousness. Therefore by παράπτωμα also is understood that sin of Adam which becomes ours by imputation, and which our natural corruption necessarily and infallibly follows. Entirely so: the Apostle does set opposite Adam's παράπτωμα and Christ's χάρισμα. What follows from that? Have we not already met several times an argument drawn from this opposition? For the rest, either this syllogism is irregular and has no force of concluding, or a proposition has been omitted which, if it is conceived universally as it ought to be, will without doubt be false. But the opposition between Adam's παράπτωμα and Christ's χάρισμα warns us that this which is ours is far otherwise than that. For it is not that, as this is ours by the gift of Christ, so that is ours by the gift of Adam. Therefore the Apostle sets the one opposite the other in the mode by which it becomes ours. How then can D. Garissoles conclude from this opposition that both become ours in the same mode? Will he say that imputation, by which something becomes ours which otherwise is not ours, is a kind of donation? Then Adam's sin is a kind of gift — not Adam's, for he does not impute; but, I shudder to pronounce it, God's own.
